entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: entity pools, restart points and three tool traps
entry.summary: A batch of 150 consecutive unnamed functions turned out to hold six different groups, and 145 of them got descriptive names. The most useful trick was reading pool-name strings out of pool constructors, which identified all seven entity pools at once.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 consecutive unnamed functions turned out to hold six different groups, and 145 of them got descriptive names. The most useful trick was reading pool-name strings out of pool constructors, which identified all seven entity pools at once.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into six groups: player-pedestrian methods, restart-point tables with save and load, weather state, allocator stubs, entity methods with the matrix pool and visibility tests, and a background probing subsystem with three work tables.

Verified Each entity pool constructor embeds its pool name as a string, which identified all seven pools: buildings, animated buildings, objects, vehicles, pedestrians, dummy pedestrians and dummy objects. The pool sizes range from 120 pedestrians to tens of thousands of buildings.

Verified Four inventory entries had wrong sizes: one vtable slot is a five-byte jump whose listed range overlaps eight neighbours, one init function tail-jumps into another, one listed function starts with the previous function's jump table and is not code at all, and one fragment continues far past its listed end.

What was decided or recommended

Verified Later naming lanes should read pool constructor strings to identify pools, cap enclosing-function attribution at about one kilobyte because far-away matches are wrong, and check operand types when scanning for references because plain immediate scans miss every memory reference.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the memory-mapped image, collect direct calls, imports and memory references per function, resolve targets against the merged symbol and lane-name tables, and confirm pool identities from the pool constructor call sites.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first evidence pass found only one string reference in the whole batch because the scanner only looked at immediate operands and missed all memory-disp references. A rescan with the correct operand type confirmed the batch genuinely has almost no string references. Caller attribution also misled several times by naming far-away native functions as callers when the true caller was an unnamed neighbour.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard row-fill functions verified; a reloc-script bug nearly deferred them all
entry.summary: All eight functions in this batch were verified against the stock checker with no failures over a thousand trials each, after two genuine rewrite bugs were found and fixed. The more useful finding is a tooling trap: a wrong handling of pefile relocation entries made the jump tables look unrelocated and the batch nearly got deferred for a checker gap that did not exist.
entry.content:
All eight functions in this batch were verified against the stock checker with no failures over a thousand trials each, after two genuine rewrite bugs were found and fixed. The more useful finding is a tooling trap: a wrong handling of pefile relocation entries made the jump tables look unrelocated and the batch nearly got deferred for a checker gap that did not exist.

What was asked

Rewrite eight medium-sized functions from the same template family in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, generating all eight from one script because they differ only in constants.

What was found

Verified The eight functions share identical logic with two parameters each: a leaderboard id constant and a row count (seven for one member, five for the rest). Each takes an object plus six stack words and returns a flag byte.

Verified Two subtle behaviours were confirmed by failing then passing trials: the function reports a stale stack-slot value, one iteration behind its cursor register, to one callee; and its key-length comparison is signed, so a negative length takes the copy path.

Verified A relocation check script added the page address twice because pefile reports each entry address already combined with its page. The corrected check shows every jump-table address in the batch is relocated, so the checker handles them normally.

What was decided or recommended

Future lanes should assert one known relocation entry before trusting any script that claims an address has none. Signedness of every comparison deserves its own audit pass: one signed greater-than among unsigned above-compares cost a full re-run here.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane generator to rebuild the eight rewrites and contracts, build the rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows, and run the stock checker driver over the eight contracts at a thousand trials each. All eight pass with their mutants caught.

What was confusing or went wrong

The wrong relocation result plus a plausible story about unrelocated reads made deferral look certain for about twenty minutes, until a probe showed most trials passing with correct dispatch. The probe data overruled the static analysis, and re-checking the script found the double-added page.

entry.title: Naming the follow cameras and the player ped
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three chase-camera classes, a camera probe-query family, shared camera math, and the player-ped class with its aim-target scanner; 143 of them are now named, most at medium confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three chase-camera classes, a camera probe-query family, shared camera math, and the player-ped class with its aim-target scanner; 143 of them are now named, most at medium confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 unnamed functions in one address run, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no guessing presented as fact.

What was found

Verified The run holds the vehicle follow camera, the on-foot follow camera, the weapon-aim camera, and the player ped, in that order, plus a vehicle camera-data loader and shared vector math.

Verified All three camera classes share vtable slot meanings: a deleting destructor, a target-entity getter, a large per-frame update, a publish step, and a deactivate step, which made the virtuals nameable with confidence.

Verified One inventory entry is not a function at all: its byte range overlaps neighbouring parser code, so it was left unnamed and flagged.

Inferred A family of about twenty functions walks four parallel probe arrays for camera collision queries; the per-element helpers they call are still unnamed, which caps the whole family at medium confidence.

What was decided or recommended

Names went into the batch file with evidence and confidence: 25 high, 118 medium, 7 left empty. The next naming lane covering nearby code should name the small physics query helpers first, since about twenty camera names depend on them.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, collect referenced strings, imported calls, known callee names and vtable slots into one table, then sweep the code section for direct callers of every batch member; the caller list was the single most useful signal after strings.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two early guesses were wrong and had to be corrected: a clamp that looked like a field-of-view limit turned out to clamp follow distance, and a timer test sits next to the health field but is not one. Both were caught by already-verified rewrites of the same functions, which are worth checking before naming anything.

entry.title: Naming a 150-function run: cleanup tables, wanted state and three shared spans
entry.summary: One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the run exposed three reusable naming signals plus three inventory spans that hold more than one function.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the run exposed three reusable naming signals plus three inventory spans that hold more than one function.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and leaving the name empty where the behaviour cannot be told.

What was found

Verified The run splits into five groups: a single network socket helper, fragment and physics lifecycle code, mission cleanup and entity creation, the wanted level system, and interiors with the follow-vehicle camera.

Verified The mission cleanup object holds two fixed tables of small entries carrying handle type, handle, owner thread and flags, and the entity-kind nibble selects the ped, vehicle or object pool.

Verified The wanted object holds a sixteen-slot crime table with position and timestamp, plus level, heat and grey-out timer fields nearby.

Verified Three inventory spans each contain more than one function: one holds switch-table data with the real function starting later, and two hold a small entry prefix with a separate function after padding.

Verified Two size-zero inventory entries are real, called functions: a fragment dirty-bit setter and a one-star wanted setter.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the destructor convention already in the merged symbols, with a plain destructor body and a deleting wrapper variant. Later lanes should name tiny single-global functions by the global effect, distrust size-zero and gapfill entries until disassembled, and add batch addresses as enclosing anchors before mapping callers, or every caller misattributes to one distant function. Tail-call callees need collecting too: the jump-based evidence pass used here misses them.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image and confirm the mapping by decoding one known function first. Build one evidence table per function with direct calls, imports, string references, a caller scan and name lookups in the merged symbols, lane names and verified rewrites, then read the short functions and the leftovers directly. The lane scratch folder keeps the scripts and tables.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first caller map attributed most calls in the interiors group to one unrelated vtable function, because no nearby function starts were known; adding the batch addresses as anchors fixed it. A helper script named after a standard library module shadowed it and crashed on import until renamed. Shell output redirection mangled one evidence dump into wide characters, so later tables were written by the scripts themselves.

entry.title: Naming a run of ped physics and playstat functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named by behaviour: 133 got names and 17 were left empty as genuinely unknown. The batch turned out to be the ped ragdoll core, network stat registration, and the playstat submitter family.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named by behaviour: 133 got names and 17 were left empty as genuinely unknown. The batch turned out to be the ped ragdoll core, network stat registration, and the playstat submitter family.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with a confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from evidence, strongest first: referenced strings, called imports, known callers and classes, then behaviour.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three groups: about a hundred ped physics and ragdoll methods, about a dozen network stat registration routines, and about thirty playstat submitters and accessors.

Verified The key that unlocked the ped group is a four-field model: the active physics instance pointer, the normal instance, the ragdoll instance, and a small ragdoll-state value. Dozens of functions test whether the active pointer equals the ragdoll one and switch between the two, which made the enter, exit, link and state names fall out directly.

Verified The health setter stores its value with three threshold flags against shared constants that read back as exactly fifty and one hundred, plus a non-positive flag.

Verified Three network routines are straight-line siblings that each register eight stats with defaults and then run an achievement check; they differ only in the stat id sets and the check slot.

Verified Every playstat class has a matched pair: one virtual slot writes the stat into a message and the other reads it back, confirmed by the verified rewrite notes and by publish-flavoured callees on one side and parse-flavoured callees on the other.

Inferred A neighbouring routine labelled as a playstat destructor is actually a timer-driven flush driver: it compares pending arrays against committed ones on tick intervals and submits what changed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Seventeen functions were left unnamed with low confidence rather than guessed, including a health-setter twin whose extra argument is never read and an entity flag setter shared by nineteen classes whose bit meaning is unknown.
  • Three inventory entries merge two or three functions into one size, and one gapfill entry jumps backward out of its own bounds; the queue should re-split them before production lanes take them.
  • The most reusable naming signals for the next lane are: native-implementation callers pin small setters, physics constructor callees reveal setup routines, and the ragdoll four-field model names a whole family at once.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: direct-call targets resolved against verified rewrites and lane names, import calls, string references, and caller sites found by scanning for relative calls and resolved to enclosing named functions. Read every small function fully, then the table-unclear ones, then name from the strongest signal.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two virtual slots do exactly the same thing with different arity, and two minimised-window-gated routines look important but their roles stayed unclear; all four were left empty. A first attempt to confirm an entity flag bit against a public SDK failed on a wrong file path and was abandoned as not worth more time. The shared constants table reads back neighbouring values alongside the target, so each constant had to be read individually rather than trusted from context.

entry.title: A call argument that changes on every run
entry.summary: Verified A function that passes a relocated address to a callee cannot have that argument compared exactly, because the checker's run of the original sits at a different base address in every worker process while the rewrite's value stays fixed. The fix is to skip that one argument and say so, after proving everything else matches.
entry.content:
Verified A function that passes a relocated address to a callee cannot have that argument compared exactly, because the checker's run of the original sits at a different base address in every worker process while the rewrite's value stays fixed. The fix is to skip that one argument and say so, after proving everything else matches.

What was asked

Routine production work: rewrite six neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each against the original with the differential checker.

What was found

Verified One function builds a table pointer from a file constant and passes it to a calibration call. The constant carries a relocation entry, so the worker patches it for wherever it placed that run's copy of the code. Two runs of the same contract, minutes apart, logged two different raw values for that argument (heap and everything else identical), which rules out nondeterminism in the function and points at the mapping base moving per worker.

Verified Unrelocated reads are unaffected: constants and zero data read through plain absolute addresses returned identical file bytes across thousands of trials and several workers, so only relocated operands need this treatment.

Inferred The logged form of the same address can also differ between the two sides (region-relative on the original side, raw on the rewrite side), which looks like a second problem but is only display: skipping the argument removes both.

What was decided or recommended

  • Skip a call argument that carries a relocated address (call_skip), and record it in the narrowed list with the reason. The skipped value in this case was still pinned down three other ways (a second call argument, a table lookup, a stored rate), so the proof lost almost nothing.
  • Do not use a bit mask to dodge it: a mask still compares values, and the values legitimately differ across runs.
  • Suspect this whenever the calls check alone fails with two different raw hex values on consecutive runs while heap, stack and return value stay green.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract whose original passes a relocated address on to a call. Run it twice and compare the logged call arguments in the two verdicts: the address argument differs while all other comparisons pass. Adding the argument to call_skip turns both runs green.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first attempt at this function also had a real rewrite bug (a matrix result subtracted instead of stored), which failed heap and calls together and hid the mapping issue until the rewrite was fixed. The region-relative versus raw display then sent the diagnosis toward the pointer comparison before the second run showed the values themselves moving. Both misdirections cost about ten minutes.

entry.title: Naming model-info pools by their stamped vtables
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the model-info manager, the portal trackers and ped virtuals, and the pool families inside it were identified completely by matching three facts: the element stride, the vtable each init stamps into its elements, and the pool header passed at the init call site.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the model-info manager, the portal trackers and ped virtuals, and the pool families inside it were identified completely by matching three facts: the element stride, the vtable each init stamps into its elements, and the pool header passed at the init call site.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from evidence.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three clusters: model-info pools with name lookup and shutdown logic, portal tracker methods with room and audio queries, and ped virtuals with task helpers.

Verified Pool headers hold a count, a used total and a base pointer. Fourteen near-identical pool inits each stamp a different class vtable, which identifies every one, including two attribute classes the batch never names directly.

Verified Five small pool getters return auxiliary pools whose contents could not be determined; they were left unnamed with their strides and callers recorded.

Inferred Two tiny callees in the encrypted first megabyte behave exactly like operator new and delete but cannot be disassembled to confirm it.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred and twenty-five functions were named, forty-eight at high confidence and seventy-seven at medium. The next naming lane facing a pool family should check stride, stamped vtable and init-site pool together before naming anything, and should re-decode tiny functions at exact size because evidence gathered past a return belongs to a neighbour.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch function, resolve direct calls and string references against the merged symbol files and verified rewrites, match stamped vtables against the class structure files, and map pool headers from the setup code in the initialiser.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two batch entries overlap: one is an alternate entry point inside the other, reached by a jump. Both were left unnamed. An external field label calling one model-info offset a float draw distance contradicts the observed increment, decrement and read behaviour, which all treat it as a reference count.

entry.title: What was really capping the lane count: 14.5 GB of kernel memory
entry.summary: With the lane target at 52, the supervisor stalled at about 14 lanes and logged "waiting for memory". Fourteen lanes do not fill a 48 GB laptop. The question was what held the rest.
entry.content:
With the lane target at 52, the supervisor stalled at about 14 lanes and logged "waiting for memory". Fourteen lanes do not fill a 48 GB laptop. The question was what held the rest.

FactValueWhat it means
Committed memory, whole system57.6 GB of a 70.6 GB limitThe supervisor's guard keeps 13 GB of headroom, so no more lanes start.
Private memory of every process added together32.3 GBAbout 25 GB of the commitment belongs to no process.
All 14 lanes' agent processes2.2 GBThe lanes are not the load.
Kernel non-paged pool14.5 GBMemory the kernel and drivers hold that can never be paged out. It counts against RAM and commitment both. On a healthy machine it is well under 2 GB.
Time since the machine was last restarted2.5 daysThe whole project so far, with well over a thousand lanes and many thousands of short-lived processes started in that time.
Committed memory with no lane running at all (4 October, 18:14)about 50 GBThe baseline was already high before this was looked at; the ceiling of "about 45 lanes" measured on 4 October was this, not the lanes' own need.

Status: the numbers above are Verified (read from the system's own counters). What is leaking is Unknown: finding the owner of pool memory needs a kernel tool that is not installed. Inferred, not shown: a driver that leaks a little for every process created would fit, because the project creates processes at a rate an ordinary desktop never does (each lane runs hundreds of builds and checker workers, and every 32-bit worker runs under emulation on this ARM64 machine). One vendor platform service holds 68,000 handles, which is unusual and may or may not be related.

Decisions

  • The health check now reports the non-paged pool and keeps each reading in a log, so the growth rate per hour and per lane started can be measured instead of guessed.
  • Only restarting the machine returns this memory. That ends every running lane and is the owner's decision; it is best done at a quota stop, when nothing is running anyway.
  • Earlier entries that blamed lane count, wrappers or other programs for memory pressure were looking at the symptom. The runaway lane script found on 4 October was real, but it was not the whole story.

To reproduce: read the system's memory counters for committed bytes and the non-paged pool, and compare with the sum of private memory over all processes.

entry.title: Lockstep test cycles can silently skip the path they were built to hit
entry.summary: A production batch of forty small streaming functions verified thirty-nine of them, and the two hardest failures were both contracts whose cycling inputs never aligned: every trial took an early exit while the target path sat untested, and only the deliberately wrong version per function exposed it.
entry.content:
A production batch of forty small streaming functions verified thirty-nine of them, and the two hardest failures were both contracts whose cycling inputs never aligned: every trial took an early exit while the target path sat untested, and only the deliberately wrong version per function exposed it.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original on the stock checker, with one wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified Thirty-nine functions passed one thousand trials each with their wrong versions caught; one was deferred because its argument-dependent conditional tail jump has no checker transport.

Verified Two contracts passed all trials while testing nothing they intended, in two different ways. First, a string-parsing function's pinned string bytes only take effect on one of three rotating heap fills, and that fill's phase never coincided with the trials that reached the store path, so the store fired zero times in sixty trials. Second, a cursor-scan function's table entries cycled valid and null out of phase with the index cycle, so every trial exited before the loops. A third contract did run its loops, but a wrap-to-zero step erased the wrong version's changed cursor on every trial, making the wrong version pass until per-slot pins forced blocked and clear slots to mix.

What was decided or recommended

Prefer fully explicit per-word heap contents over pins plus random fill for inputs a path depends on, so coverage cannot depend on fill phase. When two cycles must coincide, check the combined phase by hand for at least one trial before running. A wrong version that passes is always a contract defect to fix, never a weak wrong version to excuse: all three cases above were fixed in the contract and then caught their wrong versions.

How to reproduce it

Run any affected contract and read the coverage block of its verdict: trials where the original wrote to the heap, per-callee fire counts, and distinct call-sequence shapes. Zero heap-write trials on a function known to store, or a callee firing far less often than designed, signals a phase mismatch.

What was confusing or went wrong

The checker's run summary file is written next to the driver and overwrote the lane's own results file twice; later runs redirected driver output elsewhere and the lane file was regenerated from the verdict files at the end. A per-call answer sequence takes plain values, not pairs, which the contract validator rejects. Zero-argument callee macros require a trailing comma to compile.

entry.title: Naming a batch of loaders: display formats, pools and boundary traps
entry.summary: Naming 150 consecutive functions showed the batch is mostly data-file loading plus one mislabeled group that turned out to be display-mode enumeration, identified by exact graphics enum constants.
entry.content:
Naming 150 consecutive functions showed the batch is mostly data-file loading plus one mislabeled group that turned out to be display-mode enumeration, identified by exact graphics enum constants.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 unnamed game functions with a confidence each, working from strings, imports, callers, classes and behavior.

What was found

  • Verified A run of about thirty functions builds a display enumeration context: its init lists hold exactly the six depth-stencil formats, multisample counts zero to sixteen, and the six present intervals, and its consumer is the known display-mode collector.
  • Verified Six pool allocators map to model-info classes three ways: entry stride, pool descriptor in the verified pool-init sequence, and stamped vtable all agree.
  • Verified Thirteen vtable slot-zero functions are scalar deleting destructors in the standard shape, with per-class array strides matching the allocator strides.
  • Verified Three inventory boundaries were wrong: one size overruns into the next function, one gapfill entry is a loop block rather than a function, and three jump-stub sizes cover their neighbors.
  • Inferred Two heavily called merged names for message-sending look wrong: both slots are used as plain heap free and allocate across destructors and cleanup loops.

What was decided or recommended

Named 147 functions and left 3 empty: a non-function block and two twin processors whose backends are all unnamed. The next naming lane should re-verify weak-boundary entries with an epilogue-anchored disassembly and keep the whole-batch caller-plus-string table pass, which resolved most of this batch.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch entry, and collect import calls, referenced strings and format strings, direct callers by byte scan, and data references. Decode small functions fully, resolve unknown callees by caller count and entry shape, and check neighbor names and verified rewrite doc comments before naming.

What was confusing or went wrong

Linear disassembly through a large switch function first suggested a wrong return boundary; re-decoding from a call anchor fixed the verdict. Comparing twin functions with an oversized window produced nonsense difference counts until the true sizes were used.

entry.title: A production batch that caught the checker running corrupted code
entry.summary: Three neighbouring ped-task functions were rewritten for verification. One passed on its testable path. The other two could not be verified because the checker's worker silently rewrites their bytes before running them, applying relocation entries that do not point at addresses. The game never applies those entries, so the worker tests something the game never runs.
entry.content:
Three neighbouring ped-task functions were rewritten for verification. One passed on its testable path. The other two could not be verified because the checker's worker silently rewrites their bytes before running them, applying relocation entries that do not point at addresses. The game never applies those entries, so the worker tests something the game never runs.

What was asked

Rewrite three medium and large functions from the ped-task subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the differential checker, writing a full contract and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified The smallest function verified on its testable path: every trial agreed and the wrong version was caught. Its whole byte range contains no relocation entries, so the worker ran its true bytes.

Verified The two larger functions sit on a code page whose relocation block holds dozens of entries with targets outside the program image. The worker applies every entry, which rewrites real instructions: a stack adjustment becomes unrelated instructions that swallow the two following ones, and a switch-table address is redirected to an address that exists nowhere in the file. With byte-identical pinned inputs, trials diverged purely by heap fill pattern, which correct code cannot do.

Verified About half of all code pages contain at least one relocation entry, and only a small fraction of sampled code entries point at valid addresses. Any previously accepted rewrite whose original bytes contain such an entry was proven against corrupted code.

Verified Separately, every absolute data reference in all three functions lacks a relocation entry, including reads on unavoidable paths and an unrelocatable jump table, so two further checker abilities would still be needed after the corruption is fixed.

What was decided or recommended

The two larger functions were deferred as a checker gap, with a full contract and rewrite kept as a retry kit for one of them and a steering recipe for the other. Recommended: scan every accepted rewrite for relocation entries inside its byte range and hold out the hits, and change the worker to skip entries whose contents are not program addresses.

How to reproduce it

Compare the relocation table against the program image: entries whose four bytes do not form an address inside the image are bogus. Re-apply the table to a copy of the mapped image and disassemble the affected functions to see the rewritten instructions. Run the checker with constant steering pins and constant versus rotating heap fills to observe the impossible divergence.

What was confusing or went wrong

The fill-dependent divergence cost the most time, because every input visible to the lane was provably identical across the diverging trials. The resolution was to stop suspecting the inputs and inspect what the worker executes. A probe also ran once against a stale binary after a failed rebuild; the timestamps caught it and the run was repeated.

entry.title: Four task functions verified, and a floating-point branch trap
entry.summary: A production batch of four neighbouring task-state functions was rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent to the originals, and the work turned up a comparison trap that will bite every float-heavy rewrite: an unordered comparison result takes the same branch side as below-or-equal, so the taken side must be written as not-greater, never as less-or-equal.
entry.content:
A production batch of four neighbouring task-state functions was rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent to the originals, and the work turned up a comparison trap that will bite every float-heavy rewrite: an unordered comparison result takes the same branch side as below-or-equal, so the taken side must be written as not-greater, never as less-or-equal.

What was asked

Rewrite four medium-size functions from one game subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least a thousand generated trials, using the project's differential checker.

What was found

Verified All four functions verified with zero failures over twelve hundred trials each, and each function's deliberately wrong version was caught.

  • One function is a pure state initializer with no calls; the other three mix integer bit tests, single-precision arithmetic and up to eight outgoing calls each, including calls through object function tables.
  • Every absolute data reference in the batch is relocated normally, so no special checker ability was needed for them.
  • Two of the four proofs are narrowed in stated ways: one function passes its caller's own argument word as an out-parameter slot, which a Rust rewrite cannot name, so the stack check is off and that pointer argument is skipped; the other skips three frame-pointer call arguments while snapshotting or downstream-verifying their contents.

What was decided or recommended

Verified Float branches after a compare instruction must mirror unordered semantics exactly. The mapping that passes is:

Original branchCorrect rewrite
jump if below-or-equaltaken side is not-(a greater than b)
jump if belowtaken side is not-(a greater-or-equal b)
parity test after unordered-compareordered equality, plain == and !=

Per-trial cycling of fabricated global values uses the fill-spec cycle form; the plain values list writes consecutive addresses instead and silently overlaps when entries sit next to each other.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch's four checker contracts with the stock worker for the full trial count and confirm zero failures, no vacuous verdicts, every declared callee firing, and every wrong version failing. Feed not-a-number inputs to any float comparison covered by a below-or-equal branch and confirm both sides take the same side.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first attempt at the largest function failed on trials where the original kept a not-a-number value through a clamp that the rewrite had expressed with less-or-equal; rewriting every float branch in the not-greater form fixed all twelve failures at once. A first relocation script double-counted a table base and wrongly reported nearly every data reference as unrelocated; a raw table parse corrected it. The return value of one function looked like incidental leftovers but proved to be deterministic input-derived data on every path, so it is compared exactly rather than narrowed away.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard readers verified; unrelocated table reads work after all
entry.summary: A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard-info readers was verified end to end, and the run overturned its own triage: functions whose jump tables are read through unrelocated addresses were expected to be unverifiable on this machine, but the reads return the true table contents and every contract passed.
entry.content:
A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard-info readers was verified end to end, and the run overturned its own triage: functions whose jump tables are read through unrelocated addresses were expected to be unverifiable on this machine, but the reads return the true table contents and every contract passed.

What was asked

Rewrite eight medium-sized game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker. The eight sit next to each other and share one template shape, differing only in a leaderboard id constant and a loop bound.

What was found

Verified The eight functions are one routine instantiated eight times: identical instruction streams apart from the id constant and the bound, identical five-entry jump tables selecting a column width, and eight outgoing calls each (two through the object's own table, one id lookup with a frame-local out struct, five direct).

Verified All eight rewrites passed 1,200 trials each with no failures, none vacuous, every callee firing, and a deliberately wrong version per function caught by its contract. A second wrong version that changed only the one table entry the restricted contract never reaches passed there and failed on the full contract, showing exactly where each proof's edge lies.

Verified The jump-table reads use absolute addresses with no relocation entries, and the checker's guard window for such addresses is not held on this machine, so the batch was first triaged as unverifiable. A discriminator probe then showed the original behaving exactly as if the reads succeed: forcing the table input to one value made every trial exit the loop after exactly one iteration, which only the true table contents produce. The mechanism is still open: an external memory probe could not read the table address in the live checker process even though the running original reads it correctly on every trial.

What was decided or recommended

Verify, don't defer, functions whose only gap is an unrelocated read of game data: run one discriminator probe first, and if the original behaves as the true contents dictate, write the full contract. Batches previously deferred for this reason are worth re-running on this machine. The external-probe contradiction is recorded as an open question for the checker owners.

How to reproduce it

Generate one rewrite and one contract from the family template, forcing the table input to a single known value with the accumulator range set to zero: the original must run exactly one loop iteration per trial. Then run the full contract with per-call answer sequences that reach every table entry, with a wrong version that drops one store (must fail) and one that alters only the rarely reached entry (must fail on the full contract).

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full contract passed while silently never reaching two of the five table entries: the answer sequence that was supposed to end the loop early killed it two iterations before the entries were consumed. Counting callee firings per trial exposed the shortfall, and reordering the sequence fixed it. The external memory probe disagreeing with the in-process reads remains unexplained and is reported as unknown rather than guessed at.

entry.title: Two traps from a camera batch: a parity test that is not a NaN test, and a fault only one side sees
entry.summary: A production batch of forty small camera functions verified all forty, but two findings were surprising enough to record: a common float-compare idiom that does not mean what it looks like, and one function where the original and the rewrite provably diverge on identical inputs.
entry.content:
A production batch of forty small camera functions verified all forty, but two findings were surprising enough to record: a common float-compare idiom that does not mean what it looks like, and one function where the original and the rewrite provably diverge on identical inputs.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the checker, one wrong version per function included.

What was found

Verified The sequence compare-scalar-float, load-flags-into-ah, test-ah-with-a-mask, jump-on-parity does not test for NaN. The test instruction overwrites the parity flag with the parity of the masked-down zero and parity bits, so the jump is taken exactly when the comparison was less, greater or unordered: in short, when the float is not equal to zero. A rewrite that tested only for NaN failed; plain not-equal-to-zero matches, including NaN and both signed zeros.

Verified One dispatch function reads a mode byte through a register plus a large constant offset. With the base planted so the read lands in mapped scratch memory, the original faults at an address exactly one image-relocation delta above the planted target while the rewrite reads the planted target and succeeds; with a zero base the sides swap. Snapshots proved both sides held the same base at the preceding call, and the fault trials aligned exactly with the trials executing that instruction. The function was verified with that sub-branch excluded and disclosed; the rewrite models the file bytes and is kept for re-run.

Verified The static relocation listing disagreed with the worker twice: once where the worker demonstrably relocated an immediate the listing omits, once where the listing shows entries inside two instructions that the worker demonstrably does not apply (applying them would visibly corrupt both). Bit-level presence in that listing should not be trusted; probes decide.

What was decided or recommended

The narrowed proof stands as an honest partial result, and the divergent-fault shape is reported for a checker-side investigation before anyone re-runs the exempt path. Lanes should treat the parity-after-test idiom as not-equal, not as a NaN check, and should confirm relocation coverage by running rather than by reading the table.

How to reproduce it

Build any contract whose original reads through a register plus a large displacement with the base pinned so the sum lands in mapped heap, run it, and compare the fault address against the planted sum; and disassemble any compare-load-test-jump-on-parity float gate and evaluate the parity of each possible flag combination by hand.

What was confusing or went wrong

The divergent fault cost the most time: every mechanism checked out individually (same heap, same pins, same script answers, same path), yet the outcomes differed. Three separate misreads compounded it along the way (a branch target, a table base, the parity idiom above), each found by re-reading the bytes rather than the notes. The lesson that stuck is that when identical inputs give different terminations, the executed bytes must differ from the file bytes, and the next step is to prove that directly instead of re-checking the inputs.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: cam instructions, movie player, projectiles, cutscenes
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions split into four clean groups, and each group had one decisive naming signal: a sibling convention for the camera instructions, native callers for the movie player, a slot table for projectiles, and a callback registration for cutscenes. 137 functions got names, 13 were left empty.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions split into four clean groups, and each group had one decisive naming signal: a sibling convention for the camera instructions, native callers for the movie player, a slot table for projectiles, and a callback registration for cutscenes. 137 functions got names, 13 were left empty.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions with a confidence per name, working from strings, imports, known callers and callees, vtables and class data.

What was found

Verified The first twenty functions are one virtual method repeated across twenty camera instruction classes, and a prior lane had already named ninety of its siblings, so all twenty took the same method name at high confidence.

Verified Four tiny allocators are the factory functions for four of those instruction classes: each stores a vtable whose execute slot points at the matching instruction body, and each is called only from its matching script native.

Verified The movie player cluster resolved through its callers: the set-current, set-time and set-volume workers are each called only from the script native of the same name, and the player update mutes through a window-minimised check.

Verified Projectiles live in a fixed table of thirty-two slots. The table initialiser, per-slot cleanup, clear loops, finders and a sticky-bomb counter all reference the same table shape, which made the whole family nameable.

Verified Cutscene support centres on a manager init that registers four streaming callbacks (find-or-create, release, store, lookup), a definition-file parser recognising dozens of section tags, and a loader for the cutscene streaming format. A nearest-object search used by the area helpers passes its callback address explicitly, which confirmed both names.

Inferred A group of marker functions referencing cone, cylinder, arrow, ring and flag icon names plus a landing marker appears to set up and draw race checkpoint markers.

Unknown Thirteen functions were left unnamed, mostly because their callees sit in the encrypted first megabyte of code and read back as garbage bytes, plus one function with no callers or pointer references anywhere in the image.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the conventions prior lanes set for the same families: the execute method and factory suffix for camera instructions, and the invoke name for generic callback slots. The next naming lane covering nearby code should start from the four cutscene streaming callbacks and the projectile slot table, since neighbouring functions will reference the same structures. Unverifiable functions were left empty at low confidence rather than guessed.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the memory-mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Collect direct callees, imported functions called, referenced strings and data, then scan the code section once for direct callers and look the containing functions up in the merged name map. Verify factory-to-method links by reading the vtable slot from the image. For functions with no callers, scan the whole image for pointer references before concluding anything.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three functions initially showed a neighbour's calls and strings because the inventory size ran past the next function start; clipping evidence windows to the next start fixed it. One caller attribution fell far past its containing function and had to be discarded, so caller lookups now need a size sanity check. The inventory size of one jump stub overlaps the next four entries, and two entries with size zero hold real code. Two subsystem labels disagree with behaviour: movie code clustered as ped tasks, and identical factory functions split across two clusters.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed: the checker could not see which global word changed
entry.summary: A deliberately wrong rewrite passed one hundred trials against the original, which meant the proof could not see the change. The cause was a defect in the checker's comparison of engine globals, now reported with a contract-side workaround.
entry.content:
A deliberately wrong rewrite passed one hundred trials against the original, which meant the proof could not see the change. The cause was a defect in the checker's comparison of engine globals, now reported with a contract-side workaround.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty small script-instruction functions in Rust and prove each one against the original, with a deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified The wrong version of one function stored its value one slot off in a global array and still passed every trial. Reading the checker's comparison code showed why: for changed global words it records the declared range's base address rather than each word's own address, so two behaviours writing equal values to different words of one range compare equal. The heap, stack and undeclared-write comparisons all record per-word addresses; only the globals one has the defect. Single-word ranges are unaffected.

Verified Restating the contract with one declared range per global word closes the gap on the stock checker: the same wrong version then fails as required and the correct rewrite passes its full trial count. A second contract with a multi-word range was widened the same way before running.

Verified Two smaller findings from the same batch. One function's counter word shares its address with list slot two, so when the count is two the slot store overwrites the counter and the increment applies to the stored value; the first rewrite missed this and failed exactly the trials with that count. And one callee cleans no stack arguments while its siblings do, which the contract states explicitly.

What was decided or recommended

The defect was reported for the coordinator with the exact location and a one-line fix. Until it lands, lanes should declare one global range per word whenever a function writes more than one word of a range, and should treat any passing wrong version as a contract or checker gap to investigate, never as luck.

How to reproduce it

Take any verified contract whose rewrite writes equal values to two words of one multi-word global range, move one store to the neighbouring word in a wrong version, and run it: it passes. Split the range into one range per word and re-run: it fails.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first draft of one generator was written from crossed disassembly (three functions' listings mixed while reading chunked output). Byte-level assertions of every call site against the executable caught it before anything ran; all three were re-decoded from the file. An early relocation script also double-counted one table's base and reported nonsense until a value sample exposed it.

entry.title: Naming the script camera instruction family
entry.summary: One batch of 150 consecutive functions turned out to be almost entirely the scripted camera system: per-instruction factory functions, one execute override per instruction class, and the sequence machinery that queues and runs them. All 150 were named, and reading the sequence pump fixed the meaning of two vtable slots for the whole family at once.
entry.content:
One batch of 150 consecutive functions turned out to be almost entirely the scripted camera system: per-instruction factory functions, one execute override per instruction class, and the sequence machinery that queues and runs them. All 150 were named, and reading the sequence pump fixed the meaning of two vtable slots for the whole family at once.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into 41 instruction factories, 89 virtual execute overrides, and 20 helpers. Each factory allocates one instruction object, installs that class's vtable, stores the script arguments, and is called by exactly one script-native handler.

Verified The out-of-batch sequence pump shows what the two vtable slots mean: slot 2 runs exactly once per instruction the first time it is reached, then slot 1 is polled every frame and the sequence advances only when it reports done. So slot 2 is execute and slot 1 is a completion check. Only the wait instruction overrides slot 1, with an elapsed-time test; its execute only records the start time.

Verified The submit helper used across the subsystem appends an instruction to the open sequence when one is open, and otherwise executes it immediately and deletes it, which independently confirms the execute meaning of slot 2.

Verified Three sibling point-the-camera instruction classes share a single execute body. Two near-identical sequence-reset loops exist with different codegen, one used from init paths and one from reset paths.

Inferred A camera sequence slot holds an instruction list, a current index, a count, and a state of free, stopped, or processing, with ten slots in the manager.

What was decided or recommended

Factories follow the existing family convention with a create suffix, and every slot 2 override is named execute on its own class. The next naming lane covering instruction families should read the dispatch site first: fifteen minutes there fixed the verb for ninety functions here. Caller discovery must byte-scan for call opcodes rather than linear-sweep disassembling the code section, because the sweep desynchronises on the encrypted prefix and silently finds nothing.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per batch function with its head disassembly, referenced strings, imports called, direct callees with merged names, byte-scan callers, and data references resolved back to vtable bases and classes. Confirm each factory's class from the vtable it installs, each override's class from the vtable slot that points at it, and read the small helpers fully.

What was confusing or went wrong

Linear-sweep caller search returned zero hits for the whole batch before the encrypted-prefix desync was spotted; the byte scan then found hundreds of calls. One native-handler caller mapping carries a bogus single-letter native name, so the factory name there comes from its installed vtable instead. Two log timestamps were written from memory and one was badly wrong; the machine clock is now the only source used.

entry.title: Naming an audio-and-camera stretch: slots, hashes and fades
entry.summary: A consecutive run of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be four audio entities followed by script-camera code, and nearly all of it could be named from strings plus the script natives that call it.
entry.content:
A consecutive run of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be four audio entities followed by script-camera code, and nearly all of it could be named from strings plus the script natives that call it.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with a confidence level for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from the strongest available evidence.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into five groups: script-driven sound effects, a speech and conversation manager, weather audio, the police scanner, and script-camera helpers with screen fades.

Verified All four audio classes share parallel virtual slots: the first builds name and bank tables at registration time, one tears state down, and one runs the per-tick update. Recognising the pattern named a dozen functions at once.

Verified Three identical hash-test helpers were told apart because each guards a different conversation-line picker and scans a different global hash table.

Verified Two near-identical fade helpers were identified as fade-in and fade-out by triangulation: one is called only when clearing a cutscene, the other only when starting one, and the spawn code uses them on opposite branches.

Inferred Several merged names from earlier lanes are traps: encrypted-region stubs carry native names they only resemble, and some all-caps names are audio text tokens rather than function names. Behaviour at the call site was trusted over those labels.

What was decided or recommended

149 of 150 functions were named, about a third at high confidence and the rest at medium, with subsystem and class tags. Later lanes should keep the slot-parallel reading of the audio virtuals, keep the caller-native convention for the small camera object allocators, and distrust encrypted-stub names.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image and verify the mapping against a known function first. Gather strings, direct and import calls, byte-scan callers across the code section, data cross-references and vtable slots into one table before naming anything, then read the short and unclear functions fully.

What was confusing or went wrong

A linear-sweep disassembly of the whole code section found zero callers into the batch because decoding desynchronises; a plain byte scan for call instructions found over three hundred. One weather routine calls into the speech manager with its global object, which briefly made a speech helper look like weather code until the call setup was read.

entry.title: Naming a run of vehicle, ped and radio audio functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive audio functions were named from evidence: 54 at high confidence, 91 at medium, and 5 left unnamed where the purpose could not be pinned down.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive audio functions were named from evidence: 54 at high confidence, 91 at medium, and 5 left unnamed where the purpose could not be pinned down.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from the strongest available evidence, with a confidence grade per name.

What was found

Verified The run is the game's audio-entity code in four blocks: cutscene audio, vehicle audio with its constructor, destructor and update plus dozens of loop and one-shot helpers, ped speech and conversation helpers with a small sorting family, and radio plus script-audio routines.

Verified Class layouts from an earlier analysis lane matched the observed callers exactly: engine start-up calls the initialisers, engine shutdown calls the shutdown routines, and the per-frame updates are reached only through virtual tables, which confirmed the init, shutdown and update names independently.

Verified One-shot sound functions share a single recognisable shape and differ only in the hashed sound name, so the name string plus the caller pins each one down. Six channel-setter wrappers and three heli break-sound routines are near-identical families of this kind.

Inferred Repeated field use across the batch yields a partial map of the vehicle audio entity: bound vehicle, config handles, engine loop voices, heli damage slots, radio station and mute state, horn variant, siren damage flag and headlamp switch triggers, among others.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the project's style with the class attached where the virtual table proves it. The five functions whose purpose stayed unclear were left unnamed at low confidence rather than guessed. A speech dispatcher sitting between two batch members looks like a gap in the function inventory and was reported for the coordinator to add.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function first: referenced strings, imported calls, named callees and callers from the merged name databases, and data cross-references. Verify caller hits by decoding forward from the nearest known function start and requiring an instruction boundary exactly on the call; a plain byte scan over-attributes calls past short functions into their neighbours. Read the short bodies fully and the long ones at head and tail, then name from the strongest signal in this order: virtual-table slot with caller role, hashed sound string, native-implementation caller, shared family shape.

What was confusing or went wrong

A whole-code-section linear decode desynchronised and found zero callers; the byte-scan plus boundary-verified approach replaced it. Inventory token-hint names on some callers proved to be nearby strings rather than identities and were ignored as evidence. One caller attribution was caught overrunning a short function and is documented in the lane report.

entry.title: Leftover arguments, garbage returns, and a call the checker cannot make
entry.summary: Five of six task-system functions verified this lane; the most interesting outcomes were three calling-convention oddities in the original code and one hard checker limit that deferred the sixth function.
entry.content:
Five of six task-system functions verified this lane; the most interesting outcomes were three calling-convention oddities in the original code and one hard checker limit that deferred the sixth function.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring pedestrian-task functions in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the differential checker, one contract per function, each with its own deliberately wrong version.

What was found

Verified One function calls a helper that pops none of its three argument words, stores its floating-point result over the top word, and then calls the next helper with no new pushes, so the next helper's arguments are the previous call's leftovers plus the stored result. The checker caught my first wrong reading of this (I had the words shifted by one slot); the corrected contract passes a thousand trials with the scripted float bits compared as the next call's first argument.

Verified Another function's earliest error path returns whatever value happened to sit in the return register on entry. No rewrite can reproduce entry garbage, so the contract keeps that input non-null and the exclusion is recorded with the proof.

Verified Two functions call the same angle helper, which takes two 64-bit floats in vector registers. The checker's stack transport moves four bytes per register, so the call cannot be reproduced and the arithmetic feeding it would be unobservable. One function was verified with that branch pinned away and the callee left undeclared (reaching it would fail loudly); the other calls the helper unconditionally on every path and was deferred.

Verified Two call sites sharing one callee need two callee entries if their answers must differ: with one shared script both sites get the same answer every trial, and a mutant storing the two answers swapped passed unnoticed until the sites were split.

What was decided or recommended

  • Five functions ship as verified; the sixth is deferred with its section map and a retry kit in the lane report for when wider vector-argument transport exists.
  • Lanes should check branch-shape coverage after every mixed run: twice this lane, two gate scripts with equal periods aligned so a branch could never fire, and only the shape count revealed it.

How to reproduce it

Run this lane's five contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; each passes a thousand trials and each wrong version fails. The deferred function's report section names the unconditional call site and the worker source lines imposing the four-byte limit.

What was confusing or went wrong

The leftover-argument call took three attempts: my stack simulation read one push operand against post-push rather than pre-push state, shifting every later slot by a word. A single-trial call-log dump showed the original's actual argument words and settled it in one look. The same dump also showed scratch-register leftovers differing harmlessly between the sides, which are not compared.

entry.title: Naming a run of game audio functions
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the game audio core: occlusion, collision sounds, ped speech, ambient loops and radio emitters. One hundred thirty-five got descriptive names, twenty-eight of them high confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the game audio core: occlusion, collision sounds, ped speech, ambient loops and radio emitters. One hundred thirty-five got descriptive names, twenty-eight of them high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each function with a confidence grade.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three bands: an audio manager and occlusion core driven by curve evaluation and smoothed values, a collision and ped audio entity band, and an ambient, emitter and radio band.

Verified Eighteen identical tiny thunks each bind one slot index into a shared ped gear-jingle voice trigger; the indices run zero to seventeen with no gaps or repeats, so each thunk got a name carrying its slot number.

Verified Ten one-line speech helpers each reference a single speech line and call the ped speech routine; a crowd-reaction helper picks randomly between cheering, jeering and pain lines.

Verified Four near-identical voice release helpers differ only in which voice-handle field they release, and one of the four skips the usual audio-live gate check.

Verified The same matrix-point transform helper exists twice at different addresses, instruction for instruction.

Inferred The neon ambience controller checks whether the game window is minimized, apparently to suspend itself.

What was decided or recommended

Fifteen single-purpose setters, getters and thin forwards were left unnamed rather than given vague or slot-label names; most need the owning struct field map before they can be named. A later lane with that map should clear most of them. The duplicated transform helper should be rewritten once and shared.

How to reproduce it

An evidence script gathered referenced strings, imported calls, known callee names and data references for every function into one table first; only the short or unclear functions were then read as disassembly. Referenced strings decided about twenty-five names outright, known callee names decided most of the rest, and the class hierarchy data resolved the virtual table slots.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The main trap avoided was reading code from the raw file at mapped addresses; all reads went through the mapped image after a decode check of one known function.

entry.title: The address guard holds nothing, and constant reads pass anyway
entry.summary: A batch of four task-system functions was expected to be unverifiable because each reads data through absolute addresses the checker cannot relocate, but all three functions attempted so far verified at one thousand trials each: the guard that should make such reads fault holds zero of its 447 blocks on this machine, and the reads land on memory holding the file's own bytes.
entry.content:
A batch of four task-system functions was expected to be unverifiable because each reads data through absolute addresses the checker cannot relocate, but all three functions attempted so far verified at one thousand trials each: the guard that should make such reads fault holds zero of its 447 blocks on this machine, and the reads land on memory holding the file's own bytes.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equal to the original with the checker. The batch brief said functions reading through unrelocated absolute addresses need a checker option that does not work on this machine, and must be deferred. A first triage confirmed all four functions read that way, so the expected result was four deferrals after one confirming probe.

What was found

Verified The confirming probe passed one hundred of one hundred trials instead of faulting. A second probe forcing every trial through the absolute reads passed sixty of sixty on a fresh worker, and three full runs passed one thousand of one thousand each on further fresh workers, all bit-exact on floats and none vacuous. Every verdict records the guard holding zero blocks.

Verified The values read are the file's values: a wrong constant anywhere would fail the bit-exact comparison, and the verdicts show zero failures across six fresh worker processes.

Verified For the verified functions this is sound, not a lucky pass. The read-only constants are identical in the game by definition. The three writable-section words read as constants were scanned across the whole program text: reads only, zero writes, so the game sees the same values. One runtime pointer is pinned to its pristine null value and passed opaquely into a scripted callee; that narrowing is recorded on the result. If another machine held different bytes there, these contracts would fail loudly rather than pass wrongly.

Inferred The guard reservation fails because the system already owns that address range in every 32-bit process here, and whatever owns it on this machine has the executable's bytes mapped at the executable's addresses. The exact owner was not identified.

Function kindReadsResult
Leaf float blendread-only constants plus one never-written wordverified, 1000/1000
Probe sweep, two helpersread-only constants onlyverified, 1000/1000
Parameter clone, two callsone runtime pointer, pinned nullverified, 1000/1000 with fault parity
Large update cascadeconstants plus runtime-written wordsstaged: entry passes 1000/1000, rest planned

What was decided or recommended

The three functions are recorded as verified with the guard caveat in each result's narrowed list, where the verdict file shows it too. The large cascade is staged rather than deferred as too big: its entry plus two exits pass one thousand trials, and the remaining blocks have a written plan. Recommended: narrow the brief's deferral rule to functions reading runtime-written data, and let constants-only functions attempt verification; treat any verdict whose guard held zero blocks as carrying the caveat visibly rather than as a silent pass.

How to reproduce it

Run any contract whose original reads an unrelocated absolute constant on the stock worker and read the verdict's window record: blocks held will be zero and the trials will pass with the file's values. Scan the program text for writes to the constant's location to confirm the game cannot change it. Re-run on fresh workers to confirm stability.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first reading of the triage output was wrong: the address pattern missed short addresses, hiding most of the absolute reads, and the first relocation check tested the read targets instead of the instruction operands. Both were redone before any conclusion was drawn. The passing probe was then assumed to be a path-coverage fluke until a forced-path probe ruled that out. One table in an early draft of this entry used the wrong date from the task template; the entry is dated with the real work date.

entry.title: Naming the replay record engine: the kind byte tells siblings apart
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the replay record engine plus loading-screen render and audio timing helpers, and 127 of them could be named. The reliable signal was the record constructor each emit function funnels into: every one stamps a kind tag at the start of the record, so sibling functions that look identical are told apart by that tag.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the replay record engine plus loading-screen render and audio timing helpers, and 127 of them could be named. The reliable signal was the record constructor each emit function funnels into: every one stamps a kind tag at the start of the record, so sibling functions that look identical are told apart by that tag.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of 150 unnamed consecutive functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch holds four groups: a family of about sixty replay record-emission functions continuing the previous batch, replay table and clip-state helpers including the load and save worker threads, a few loading-screen render functions, and a tail of timing-list and audio-spatial helpers.

Verified Every emission constructor stamps a kind tag byte at the start of its record. Decoding the first instructions of the unnamed constructors gave a kind map that separates otherwise identical siblings, including a particle-effects group that shares one kind with flag-bit sub-variants.

Verified Two inventory sizes are short: a handle-release function and a match-table search both run past their listed end. Both were named for their entry points.

Inferred The slot-ring machinery is treated as the replay clip recorder, following the previous naming batch: audio, physics and particle callers record their events into clips. An alternative reading, that the ring belongs to the audio engine itself, is left open.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established replay prefix convention. Twenty-three functions were left empty at low confidence, mostly emits whose kind tag and caller give no event semantics. The next naming lane in this area should decode constructor kind tags first, before reading full disassembly.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped executable image, resolve direct calls against the verified rewrites and lane names, scan all call sites for callers with an in-range check against the function inventory, and decode the first instructions of each unnamed record constructor to read its kind tag.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest inventory entry misattributes a few call sites to short neighbouring functions, confirming the previous lane's warning; every attribution was range-checked and the failures treated as unknown callers. The subsystem hint labels on the batch were wrong for the large majority of functions.
