entry.title: Naming 150 audio and frontend functions: slot patterns worth reusing
entry.summary: Named 131 of 150 consecutive audio and frontend functions; the 19 left unnamed are bare field accesses, four large float kernels of unclear role, and one inventory entry that is not a function at all.
entry.content:
Named 131 of 150 consecutive audio and frontend functions; the 19 left unnamed are bare field accesses, four large float kernels of unclear role, and one inventory entry that is not a function at all.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names with confidence levels for a batch of 150 unnamed consecutive functions, working out what the group is about first. Only names, no rewrites.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into four groups: two sound-voice backend classes with near-identical twin methods, three sound-graph node classes with their tick helpers and trampolines, the DSP effect family with its platform backends and the voice render path, and the frontend menu and input code.

Verified Three slot patterns repeat across whole class families and can be reused directly by other naming lanes. In the effect family, the initialise slot runs a shared base setup then installs per-effect defaults, the refresh slot cycles an index and updates a parameter block, one slot is always a five-instruction address computation, and the advance slot rotates a table row then hands control to a linked stage. In the platform DSP backends the three slots are initialise, free buffers, and process samples. In sound-graph nodes the behaviour slot validates, binds operands, then creates a child.

Verified One inventory entry is a mis-split: its first bytes are a jump-table case belonging to the previous function, followed by padding, with the real code starting partway in. It was left unnamed with that evidence so no production lane treats the entry bytes as a body.

Inferred The small status queries on voice objects were named literally for what they test rather than for a guessed purpose such as playing or finished, and one single-call forward was left unnamed because play and stop read identically.

What was decided or recommended

Next naming lanes on nearby batches should expect the same twin structure: ADPCM voice methods mirror the plain ones at different field offsets, and the display-mode layout pickers repeat one code shape with different table ids. Caller addresses found by byte scan must be validated against the code section bounds, because identical byte patterns in data sections produce bogus callers.

How to reproduce it

All work used mapped reads of the executable through pefile, capstone disassembly, string and import cross-references, caller and vtable-pointer scans, the verified rewrite doc comments for overlapping addresses, and the audio class-layout tables. The scripts and the per-function evidence table stay in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early version of the gather script indexed the memory-mapped image by file offset instead of by relative virtual address, which silently produced wrong pointer-reference addresses; a check decodes one known function end to end caught it before any naming used the data. Two large float kernels in the voice render path were left unnamed after their callers and callees still did not pin down their exact role.

entry.title: Merging the cloud review, and three traps on the way to checker version 5
entry.summary: A cloud session reviewed the repository for most of a day without the game's files and opened a pull request of 85 commits: trust tooling for the rewrites, checker version 5, the assembly of verified rewrites, the first crates of the lift, a shader translator, new site pages and a wider pipeline. The question was how to merge it under a swarm that commits every five minutes and whose lanes call the tracked checker driver directly. This entry records what was checked, what went wrong while checking, and what was decided.
entry.content:
A cloud session reviewed the repository for most of a day without the game's files and opened a pull request of 85 commits: trust tooling for the rewrites, checker version 5, the assembly of verified rewrites, the first crates of the lift, a shader translator, new site pages and a wider pipeline. The question was how to merge it under a swarm that commits every five minutes and whose lanes call the tracked checker driver directly. This entry records what was checked, what went wrong while checking, and what was decided.

QuestionFindingStatus
Does version 5 give the same verdicts as version 4 on this machine?Yes: all 38 existing proofs and all 34 wrong versions match the verdicts on record. Run twice, once from the branch and once from main after the merge.Verified
Do the new abilities work here?x87 entry values and state, vector arguments beyond the second, and snapshots of up to 64 words: their five proofs pass and their wrong versions are caught. The guard proof that is meant to fail does fail.Verified
Does the read-only shadow option work here?No. It needs the worker to hold the address range the original was linked for. In every 32-bit process on this machine (Windows on ARM64, running x86 code under emulation) a system mapping already holds that whole range before the worker's first instruction; the worker holds none of it. A fresh worker never helps, so the driver's retries cannot succeed.Verified (three fresh processes inspected, and the version 4 worker for comparison)
Is the guard still sound when the worker holds none of the range?On this machine, yes: the range is reserved and not readable, so an unrelocated read by the original faults, which is what the guard is for. That is a property of this machine, not something the worker ensured.Inferred from the guard proof failing with a fault on the original's side

Trap 1: a build that was not rebuilt

The branch was unpacked into a scratch folder from a git archive and built into its own output folder, so that nothing live was touched. The first regression then reported that the new proofs were missing from the proof library. The library was stale: an earlier, failed attempt had built the live tree's library into the same output folder, and files unpacked from an archive carry the time of the commit, which was older than that output. The build tool compares times, judged the library current and did not rebuild it. Cleaning the two crates and building again fixed it. A regression that had seemed to say "33 of 38 match, then a crash" was really a version 5 worker running a version 4 proof library. Rule: after unpacking sources from an archive into a build folder that has been used before, clean first.

Trap 2: "nothing changes for the lanes" was wrong

The plan was to merge and leave the live worker on version 4 until version 5 was proven. But lanes do not only run the worker: they run the tracked driver script and build their rewrites against the tracked runtime crate. A merge would have changed both under thirty running lanes while the worker stayed old. The first answer was a merge that held those files back; a trial of it broke the new ledger, which imports a new checker script. Before a second, narrower hold-back was needed, the problem went away for another reason (next section): with no lane running, the whole branch could be merged and the worker swapped in the same quiet window.

Trap 3: the quota ran out, and the supervisor did not notice

At 17:42 every lane ended within three minutes with the model service's "quota exhausted" error; the message gives the reset time. The supervisor saw free slots and kept starting two lanes a pass, each of which failed at once and took a batch of functions with it. Setting its target to zero did nothing, because it reads a zero as "not set"; the stop file did. Thirty-six lanes ended this way. Their batches, and those of older stopped lanes, are covered by the next finding.

A release step that never released

The tick gives back the batch of a lane that stopped without results. It decided "without results" by whether the lane's folder held a results file. The checker driver writes a file of that same name into the folder it runs in, so most stopped lanes looked as if they had results, and their batches stayed reserved for good. The step now keeps only what a lane settled (verified, or deferred with a reason) and what is already in the verified tree, and never removes a lane's list, because lane numbers are taken from the lists. Its first run handed back 948 functions from 68 stopped lanes.

Decisions

  • The pull request was merged whole at 17:51 with a merge commit, after the trial merge, the script tests, the publication check and the ledger check passed on the merged tree. The worker and proof library were swapped at 17:55; version 4's are kept beside them.
  • The production brief is version b9: it names the new abilities and tells lanes that the shadow option cannot work here, with the deferral reason to record.
  • The tick now regenerates the site's history, quality and feed data.
  • Still open: the supervisor should stop by itself when lanes fail with a quota error; the shadow option needs a different design on this machine (placing the shadow inside the system's reservation, or running those proofs on an x64 machine).

To reproduce the address-range finding: start the 32-bit worker, and from another process list the regions of its address space between the original's preferred base and the end of its image; they are one reserved, mapped region whose allocation begins far below the range.

entry.title: Naming batch 55: animation channel slots, input devices, drawable parsing
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions across animation channels, DirectInput handling, model drawables, JPEG codec glue and graphics setup are now named, with six left explicitly unnamed where the purpose could not be determined.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions across animation channels, DirectInput handling, model drawables, JPEG codec glue and graphics setup are now named, with six left explicitly unnamed where the purpose could not be determined.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of unnamed game functions, working out what each address group is about first and grading every name with a confidence.

What was found

Verified The animation channel classes share one vtable layout whose slots now have meanings: object deletion, cloning, per-type sampling at a frame time, an adopt-or-compress slot, an allocation-size slot and a resource serializer. Static channels compress by uniformity check, curve channels by recursive least-squares fitting, run-length channels by rice encoding.

Verified The keyboard and mouse initializers are pinned by their DirectInput device identifiers, the gamepad path by its XInput library strings, and a control-map save and load pair by a four-letter stream magic.

Verified The drawable section parsers are pinned by their keywords: version header, skeleton, joint limits, bounding center and radius. One frustum test calls the named frustum helper.

Verified Six JPEG glue functions are the standard image-library source and destination callbacks, recognized by the fake end-of-image marker written on stream exhaustion and by the five-callback install shape.

Verified Three symbol-table entries labelled as fragment-drawable deleting destructors are actually multiple-inheritance thunks that adjust the object pointer and call into the draw workers.

What was decided or recommended

Naming lanes should read the actual virtual tables rather than trusting slot labels, check sibling lanes for per-family vocabulary before inventing names, and treat any deleting-destructor label as guilty until the disassembly shows a free. The stream read and write helpers are now pinned by direction, which future serializer lanes can rely on.

How to reproduce it

All evidence was gathered with mapped-image reads and a linear disassembler: per-function tables of calls, imports, string references and data references, verified-rewrite doc comments for sibling slots, virtual-table dumps, and direct reads of the short functions. The batch evidence table and full disassembly stay in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

One batch entry spans four entry points (a draw slot plus three co-located thunks), so it is named for its primary slot with the sharing noted. Two composite fan-out functions call a slot on every child drawable but no evidence says to what end, so they are unnamed rather than guessed. A six-byte jump into the encrypted code prefix is likewise unnamed.

entry.title: A callee that pops more than its call site pushes
entry.summary: Verifying a batch of ped-task functions turned up a case every lane should check for: a helper that pops five words while its call site pushes only two, because three floating-point arguments are stored above the stack pointer before the pushes. The checker cannot catch a wrong argument count here, so I verified all 35 callees in the batch independently.
entry.content:
Verifying a batch of ped-task functions turned up a case every lane should check for: a helper that pops five words while its call site pushes only two, because three floating-point arguments are stored above the stack pointer before the pushes. The checker cannot catch a wrong argument count here, so I verified all 35 callees in the batch independently.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring task-system functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original, including the largest one, a 780-byte updater with fifteen callees and five global tables.

What was found

Verified All eight functions verified at 1200 trials each with every mutant caught.

Verified One helper pops five words where its call site pushes two. The remaining three arguments are constant floats stored before the pushes, so the declaration genuinely has five parameters and the rewrite must push all five. A nearby stack read only makes sense with the five-word cleanup: with two it would read a caller-saved register instead of the intended table index.

Verified The checker's call stubs pop the argument count from the contract on both sides, so a wrong count is invisible to every check while silently moving the post-call stack. Any function whose code reads stack slots after a stubbed call needs its callees' true cleanups confirmed outside the checker.

What was decided or recommended

All 35 direct callees in the batch had their true cleanup sizes decoded by following control flow from each entry to its returns, and every one matches its contract. Lanes should run the same audit wherever post-call code reads stack-relative slots: count pushes at the call site is not enough, because arguments can be pre-stored.

How to reproduce it

Decode each callee recursively from its entry, collecting every reachable return and its pop count, and compare with the contract's argument count. Separately, inspect each call site for stores to outgoing stack slots above the pre-push stack pointer. Where the two disagree, the callee's epilogue wins and the contract must declare the full count.

What was confusing or went wrong

The tail index first looked like an incoming callee-saved register, which no worker transport can deliver to a rewrite and which would have made the function unverifiable. Three hand stack traces agreed on that reading before the epilogue decode showed the five-word cleanup and settled it as a plain local. A linear sweep had also suggested a wrong pop count for one small helper; the control-flow decode corrected it.

entry.title: Naming the animation channel region: slot table, cache slots, compressor
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive animation functions were all named, most at high confidence, by decoding the channel vtable slots once and reusing them everywhere, and by scanning for callers to pin down four cache entry points.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive animation functions were all named, most at high confidence, by decoding the channel vtable slots once and reusing them everywhere, and by scanning for callers to pin down four cache entry points.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch is one animation region in five groups: tolerance and channel-group lifecycle, channel base and raw channel methods, a mutex-guarded animation cache, creature mover and skeleton components, and channel bit tools with the remaining channel subclasses.

Verified The channel vtable slots are consistent across eleven subclasses: destructor, heap clone, per-type frame samplers, per-type indexed samplers, a double-returning float evaluator, per-type try-build-from-samples returning success, storage size, and serialize. The base indexed samplers just convert the index to a frame and tail-call the frame sampler.

Verified Track compression picks the smallest encoding that succeeds: the float picker tries static, delta, quantized and raw builds, and the integer worker tries three integer builds the same way. Vector and quaternion tracks first try a static collapse, then per-component float builds or raw keys depending on version.

Verified Four near-identical cache find-or-create functions serve different users: degree-of-freedom data, float channels, animation tracks, and the dispatch path, with nine, three, nine and thirteen callers respectively.

Inferred A further channel type id seen in the integer picker belongs to a run-length-encoded integer channel class referenced by nearby callers.

What was decided or recommended

Later naming lanes covering channel subclasses should reuse this slot table instead of re-deriving it, and should run a caller scan before reading big functions: caller names decided the merge, clone, rebase and cache names here. The inventory subsystem labels split this region into three; all of it is animation code.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble through the mapped image with the standard toolchain, diff same-size neighbours to find family parameters, read verified rewrite doc comments for functions already rewritten in range, and byte-scan nearby clean code for direct calls into the batch to attribute callers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Early helper lookups returned garbage disassembly until it became clear the callees sit in the encrypted first megabyte of code; behaviours depending on them were named from the readable side only. One batch entry overlaps the following functions because its recorded size counts padding, so disassembly extents were checked by hand there.
